title: PrimFlow: Learning Trajectory Primitives for Few-Step Distillation

paper.title: PrimFlow : Learning Trajectory Primitives for Few-Step Distillation
paper.abstract: Abstract Few-step trajectory distillation aims to learn accurate global updates from dense local supervision along a teacher’s sampling trajectory. Existing approaches construct within-step dynamics using specific trajectory parameterizations or discrete interval predictions, tying the learned update to a prescribed temporal structure. We propose PrimFlow , which directly learns a continuous trajectory primitive representing cumulative displacement along the teacher trajectory. By supervising finite differences of the primitive with local teacher velocities, PrimFlow learns the accumulated motion directly, while obtaining global updates through endpoint differences. This formulation avoids prescribing a temporal basis or fixed query grid and instead learns the temporal evolution of cumulative displacement from local supervision. We further establish a local-to-global error bound to characterize how local regression errors affect full-interval displacement accuracy, and introduce endpoint absorption to eliminate the auxiliary primitive branch while preserving one-network-evaluation inference. Experiments on large-scale text-to-image generation show that PrimFlow achieves a T-FID of 20.92 and an HPSv2 score of 28.35 at one NFE, improving both metrics over a trajectory-distillation baseline. After endpoint absorption, it retains comparable performance, achieving a T-FID of 20.86 and an HPSv2 score of 28.33.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow matching models have achieved remarkable success in high-quality visual generation ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) . However, their iterative sampling procedures require many neural function evaluations (NFEs), motivating few-step distillation methods that transfer a pretrained teacher’s behavior to a student with substantially fewer evaluations ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ) . In trajectory distillation, the teacher provides dense local supervision along its sampling trajectory, while the student must reproduce the accumulated motion over much larger time intervals. How to represent within-step dynamics so that local teacher supervision can effectively guide the learning of global updates remains a central challenge. Recent trajectory distillation methods address this challenge through different mechanisms for modeling within-step dynamics. π \pi -Flow ( Chen et al., 2026 ) learns an intra-step policy whose rollout generates a trajectory, ArcFlow ( Yang et al., 2026 ) parameterizes velocity evolution using analytically integrable momentum modes, and PDD ( Shaul et al., 2026 ) predicts multiple subinterval quantities in parallel. These methods construct within-step motion through policy-based trajectory generation, prescribed velocity parameterization, or discrete interval prediction. This observation motivates a direct alternative: can we learn a continuous cumulative-displacement function directly from local teacher supervision, rather than constructing within-step dynamics through a prescribed velocity parameterization, policy rollout, or discrete interval predictions? Such a formulation would let the temporal shape of cumulative displacement be learned from the teacher signals themselves, without committing it to one of these constructions. In this work, we propose PrimFlow , which directly learns cumulative displacement as a continuous function of time. Local teacher velocities supervise finite differences of this function over short intervals, while the displacement over any interval is obtained directly from the difference between its endpoint values. This allows a single learned function to support both local trajectory supervision and global student updates, without requiring a predefined temporal basis or fixed query grid. We further analyze the proposed local supervision scheme and establish a local-to-global error bound relating local regression errors to full-interval displacement errors under smoothness and partition assumptions. For efficient deployment, we introduce endpoint absorption, which transfers the learned endpoint update into the native prediction head and removes the auxiliary primitive branch while preserving one-NFE inference. Experiments on large-scale text-to-image generation show that PrimFlow achieves a T-FID of 20.92 and an HPSv2 score of 28.35 at one NFE, compared with 23.55 and 27.71 for our reproduced trajectory-distillation baseline. After endpoint absorption, the corresponding scores are 20.86 and 28.33. Our main contributions are as follows: • We introduce PrimFlow , which directly learns a continuous cumulative-displacement function for trajectory distillation, reducing reliance on predefined mechanisms for constructing within-step dynamics. • We formulate local finite-difference supervision for learning cumulative displacement and analyze its relationship to global displacement accuracy through a local-to-global error bound. • We introduce endpoint absorption for branch-free, one-NFE deployment and obtain lower T-FID and higher HPSv2 than a reproduced trajectory-distillation baseline.

sections.heading: Diffusion models.
sections.text: Diffusion models generate data by reversing a gradual noising process, typically through a stochastic differential equation or its probability-flow ODE Ho et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2021) . Flow matching provides a simulation-free alternative for learning the corresponding continuous velocity field by regressing conditional probability paths Lipman et al. (2023) . Rectified flow adopts a linear coupling between data and noise and progressively straightens the induced transport paths Liu et al. (2023) . These formulations have enabled high-quality visual generation, but inference still requires repeated velocity evaluations along the reverse trajectory. InstaFlow applies reflow to large text-to-image models and demonstrates that a sufficiently straightened flow can be distilled into a one-step generator Liu et al. (2024) .

sections.heading: Few-step distillation.
sections.text: Progressive distillation repeatedly halves the number of sampling steps Salimans and Ho (2022) , while consistency models enforce agreement among predictions from states on the same probability-flow trajectory Song et al. (2023) . DMD and DMD2 instead optimize one-step generators through distribution matching Yin et al. (2024b) ; Yin et al. (2024a) , and Trajectory Distribution Matching combines marginal alignment with trajectory-level supervision Luo et al. (2025) . Recent methods expose richer within-step dynamics: MeanFlow predicts a two-time average velocity Geng et al. (2025) , π \pi -Flow learns an intra-step policy Chen et al. (2026) , ArcFlow uses analytically integrable momentum modes Yang et al. (2026) , and PDD predicts multiple subinterval quantities in parallel Shaul et al. (2026) . These approaches specify different temporal function families or assembly rules for teacher trajectories; PrimFlow instead takes the cumulative trajectory primitive as the primary learned object.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: PrimFlow learns one continuous trajectory primitive from local teacher velocities and uses its endpoint to form the coarse student update. We first identify the shared local-to-global structure, then parameterize and learn the primitive before transferring its endpoint to the native prediction head.

sections.heading: 3.2 Local and Global Integrals in Trajectory Distillation
sections.text: Along a fixed teacher trajectory, local and global motion are two scales of the same integral. The local displacement and average velocity are given by Eq. ( 4 ); during training, pointwise teacher velocities supervise predictions of these short-interval averages. Inference instead requires the average over the complete coarse step, v ¯ s → r ⋆ = 1 s − r ​ ∫ r s v ϕ ​ ( z σ , σ , c ) ​ 𝑑 σ , z r = z s − ( s − r ) ​ v ¯ s → r ⋆ . \bar{v}^{\star}_{s\rightarrow r}=\frac{1}{s-r}\int_{r}^{s}v_{\phi}(z_{\sigma},\sigma;c)\,d\sigma,\qquad z_{r}=z_{s}-(s-r)\bar{v}^{\star}_{s\rightarrow r}. (6) For a partition s = σ 0 > σ 1 > ⋯ > σ m = r s=\sigma_{0}>\sigma_{1}>\cdots>\sigma_{m}=r , the global average is the interval-length-weighted combination of the local averages: v ¯ s → r ⋆ = ∑ i = 1 m Δ i s − r ​ v ¯ σ i − 1 → σ i ⋆ , Δ i := σ i − 1 − σ i . \bar{v}^{\star}_{s\rightarrow r}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{\Delta_{i}}{s-r}\,\bar{v}^{\star}_{\sigma_{i-1}\rightarrow\sigma_{i}},\qquad\Delta_{i}:=\sigma_{i-1}-\sigma_{i}. Existing methods differ in the intermediate object used to realize it: an average-velocity predictor, an analytically integrable temporal family, a set of grid-wise interval predictions, or a sequentially rolled-out trajectory ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Shaul et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . PrimFlow instead represents the integrals themselves through a continuous primitive, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Figure 1: Representing within-step trajectory geometry. A prescribed temporal family or fixed interval grid constrains how the teacher trajectory is represented. PrimFlow directly represents interval integrals as differences of one source-anchored continuous primitive.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments evaluate the learned primitive endpoint against a matched trajectory-distillation baseline and then examine its transfer to the native head for 1-NFE deployment.

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: We instantiate PrimFlow on a FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B rectified-flow text-to-image teacher–student pair at 1024 2 1024^{2} resolution using prompts from Lakonik/t2i-prompts-3m. The backbone is adapted with rank-256 LoRA. The tokenwise primitive branch uses eight gated residual blocks of width 512, sinusoidal start/query embeddings, and an expansion ratio of four, for 25.80M parameters. Each example samples K = 8 K=8 local windows spanning three of 128 raw-time substeps; the first 250 data-loading iterations shift the sampled states from teacher-advanced to detached student-advanced trajectories. We train with AdamW8bit at learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , loss scale 30, guidance scale 4.0, and EMA.

sections.heading: Matched comparison.
sections.text: We compare with a reproduced ArcFlow model because it also learns within-step trajectory dynamics and can use the same teacher and local supervision pipeline. Both methods use the same frozen teacher, prompt dataset, rank-256 LoRA locations, eight online teacher-velocity targets per example, and evaluation protocol. Both are trained for 2,500 iterations on four nodes (32 GPUs). ArcFlow uses 16 Gaussian momentum modes; PrimFlow replaces that temporal parameterization with the shared primitive. All reported distilled-model results use seed 1.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: T-FID is the Fréchet distance between InceptionV3 pool3 features from 3,200 student images and 3,200 images from the 50-step teacher, generated with the same prompts and initial noise. HPSv2 measures human-preference-aligned text–image quality. GenEval evaluates compositional correctness on 553 prompts and 2,212 images, and DPG-Bench provides a complementary prompt-following score. The 50-step teacher is evaluated with the same suite.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced PrimFlow from a simple view of trajectory distillation: the quantity connecting dense local velocities to a few-step update is their cumulative displacement. By making this quantity the learned object, a continuous primitive can acquire its temporal evolution from local finite differences without committing it to a prescribed temporal family or trajectory-construction procedure. Our analysis relates these local errors to full-interval displacement under smoothness and partition assumptions. Endpoint absorption further shows that this flexible training representation need not alter the deployed model: its endpoint update can be transferred to the native head, leaving the original one-NFE inference graph. On large-scale text-to-image generation, this formulation yields lower T-FID and higher HPSv2 than the reproduced trajectory-distillation baseline, with both metrics retained after absorption. More broadly, PrimFlow provides a direct route from local trajectory supervision to efficient global-update learning.

Recent trajectory distillation methods address this challenge through different mechanisms for modeling within-step dynamics. π \pi -Flow ( Chen et al., 2026 ) learns an intra-step policy whose rollout generates a trajectory, ArcFlow ( Yang et al., 2026 ) parameterizes velocity evolution using analytically integrable momentum modes, and PDD ( Shaul et al., 2026 ) predicts multiple subinterval quantities in parallel. These methods construct within-step motion through policy-based trajectory generation, prescribed velocity parameterization, or discrete interval prediction. This observation motivates a direct alternative: can we learn a continuous cumulative-displacement function directly from local teacher supervision, rather than constructing within-step dynamics through a prescribed velocity parameterization, policy rollout, or discrete interval predictions? Such a formulation would let the temporal shape of cumulative displacement be learned from the teacher signals themselves, without committing it to one of these constructions. In this work, we propose PrimFlow , which directly learns cumulative displacement as a continuous function of time. Local teacher velocities supervise finite differences of this function over short intervals, while the displacement over any interval is obtained directly from the difference between its endpoint values. This allows a single learned function to support both local trajectory supervision and global student updates, without requiring a predefined temporal basis or fixed query grid. We further analyze the proposed local supervision scheme and establish a local-to-global error bound relating local regression errors to full-interval displacement errors under smoothness and partition assumptions. For efficient deployment, we introduce endpoint absorption, which transfers the learned endpoint update into the native prediction head and removes the auxiliary primitive branch while preserving one-NFE inference. Experiments on large-scale text-to-image generation show that PrimFlow achieves a T-FID of 20.92 and an HPSv2 score of 28.35 at one NFE, compared with 23.55 and 27.71 for our reproduced trajectory-distillation baseline. After endpoint absorption, the corresponding scores are 20.86 and 28.33. Our main contributions are as follows: • We introduce PrimFlow , which directly learns a continuous cumulative-displacement function for trajectory distillation, reducing reliance on predefined mechanisms for constructing within-step dynamics. • We formulate local finite-difference supervision for learning cumulative displacement and analyze its relationship to global displacement accuracy through a local-to-global error bound. • We introduce endpoint absorption for branch-free, one-NFE deployment and obtain lower T-FID and higher HPSv2 than a reproduced trajectory-distillation baseline. 2 Related Work Diffusion models. Diffusion models generate data by reversing a gradual noising process, typically through a stochastic differential equation or its probability-flow ODE Ho et al. (2020) ; Song et al. (2021) . Flow matching provides a simulation-free alternative for learning the corresponding continuous velocity field by regressing conditional probability paths Lipman et al. (2023) . Rectified flow adopts a linear coupling between data and noise and progressively straightens the induced transport paths Liu et al. (2023) . These formulations have enabled high-quality visual generation, but inference still requires repeated velocity evaluations along the reverse trajectory. InstaFlow applies reflow to large text-to-image models and demonstrates that a sufficiently straightened flow can be distilled into a one-step generator Liu et al. (2024) . Few-step distillation. Progressive distillation repeatedly halves the number of sampling steps Salimans and Ho (2022) , while consistency models enforce agreement among predictions from states on the same probability-flow trajectory Song et al. (2023) . DMD and DMD2 instead optimize one-step generators through distribution matching Yin et al. (2024b) ; Yin et al. (2024a) , and Trajectory Distribution Matching combines marginal alignment with trajectory-level supervision Luo et al. (2025) . Recent methods expose richer within-step dynamics: MeanFlow predicts a two-time average velocity Geng et al. (2025) , π \pi -Flow learns an intra-step policy Chen et al. (2026) , ArcFlow uses analytically integrable momentum modes Yang et al. (2026) , and PDD predicts multiple subinterval quantities in parallel Shaul et al. (2026) . These approaches specify different temporal function families or assembly rules for teacher trajectories; PrimFlow instead takes the cumulative trajectory primitive as the primary learned object. 3 Method PrimFlow learns one continuous trajectory primitive from local teacher velocities and uses its endpoint to form the coarse student update. We instantiate PrimFlow on a FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B rectified-flow text-to-image teacher–student pair at 1024 2 1024^{2} resolution using prompts from Lakonik/t2i-prompts-3m. The backbone is adapted with rank-256 LoRA. The tokenwise primitive branch uses eight gated residual blocks of width 512, sinusoidal start/query embeddings, and an expansion ratio of four, for 25.80M parameters. Each example samples K = 8 K=8 local windows spanning three of 128 raw-time substeps; the first 250 data-loading iterations shift the sampled states from teacher-advanced to detached student-advanced trajectories. We train with AdamW8bit at learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , loss scale 30, guidance scale 4.0, and EMA. Matched comparison. We compare with a reproduced ArcFlow model because it also learns within-step trajectory dynamics and can use the same teacher and local supervision pipeline. Both methods use the same frozen teacher, prompt dataset, rank-256 LoRA locations, eight online teacher-velocity targets per example, and evaluation protocol. Both are trained for 2,500 iterations on four nodes (32 GPUs). ArcFlow uses 16 Gaussian momentum modes; PrimFlow replaces that temporal parameterization with the shared primitive. All reported distilled-model results use seed 1. Metrics. T-FID is the Fréchet distance between InceptionV3 pool3 features from 3,200 student images and 3,200 images from the 50-step teacher, generated with the same prompts and initial noise. HPSv2 measures human-preference-aligned text–image quality. GenEval evaluates compositional correctness on 553 prompts and 2,212 images, and DPG-Bench provides a complementary prompt-following score. The 50-step teacher is evaluated with the same suite. 4.2 Main comparison Table 1 evaluates the trajectory-trained model through its primitive endpoint before absorption. By making this quantity the learned object, a continuous primitive can acquire its temporal evolution from local finite differences without committing it to a prescribed temporal family or trajectory-construction procedure. Our analysis relates these local errors to full-interval displacement under smoothness and partition assumptions. Endpoint absorption further shows that this flexible training representation need not alter the deployed model: its endpoint update can be transferred to the native head, leaving the original one-NFE inference graph. On large-scale text-to-image generation, this formulation yields lower T-FID and higher HPSv2 than the reproduced trajectory-distillation baseline, with both metrics retained after absorption. More broadly, PrimFlow provides a direct route from local trajectory supervision to efficient global-update learning. References Chen et al. (2026) H. Chen, K. Zhang, H. Tan, L. Guibas, G.
